title: HE DIDN’T STEAL THE MONEY. HE DIDN’T LOSE IT. HE BURIED IT. SO WHY DID JESUS CALL HIM WICKED?
paragraphs: HE DIDN’T STEAL THE MONEY. HE DIDN’T LOSE IT. HE BURIED IT. SO WHY DID JESUS CALL HIM WICKED?
The Terrifying Truth Behind the Servant Who Hid His Talent — And Why Matthew 25:14–30 May Expose Something We Have Been Hiding From God for Years.
He didn't run away with his master's money.
He didn't spend it on prostitutes, gambling, or a life of reckless pleasure.
He didn't steal a single coin.
When his master returned, every bit of what had been entrusted to him was still there.
Safe.
Untouched.
Accounted for.
And yet, he heard words no servant would ever want to hear.
“You wicked and slothful servant!” — Matthew 25:26 (KJV)
Then came the sentence.
His talent was taken away. He was cast into the outer darkness, where there would be weeping and gnashing of teeth.
And suddenly, the question becomes deeply uncomfortable.
How could a man who lost nothing end up losing everything?
Because what if the most dangerous thing about his story was not what he did wrong...
But what he refused to do at all?
And what if Jesus told this parable because He knew there would be people who would spend their entire lives avoiding obvious scandals while quietly refusing the very Lord they claimed to serve?
People who never openly rejected God.
Never publicly renounced their faith.
Never declared themselves enemies of Christ.
They simply buried what had been entrusted to them.
And called it being careful.
Before we go any further, we need to understand something important.

This parable is not merely a motivational speech about using your abilities. It is not Jesus telling people to become wealthy, build successful businesses, or prove their worth through impressive achievements.
It is a warning about the return of the Master.
And it is about something far more serious than money.
It is about what our response to the Master reveals about our hearts.
Jesus tells this story in Matthew 25, during His teaching about readiness, faithfulness, and the coming judgment.

In the chapter before it, He has been speaking about His return. Immediately before this parable, He tells the story of ten virgins, five wise and five foolish. Immediately afterward, He speaks of the Son of Man coming in glory and separating the sheep from the goats.
This is not accidental.
Jesus is calling people to live faithfully while they await His return.
And then He tells a story about a man going on a journey.
Before leaving, the man calls his servants and entrusts his possessions to them.
One receives five talents.
Another receives two.
The third receives one.
Matthew tells us that each received according to his ability.
Now, here is where we must correct a common misunderstanding.
The Greek word translated “talent” is τάλαντον (talanton).
In this passage, it does not originally mean a natural ability such as singing, writing, teaching, or preaching.
It refers to a substantial unit of monetary weight or value.
A single talent represented an enormous amount of money. Depending on the historical reckoning, it could be roughly equivalent to several thousand days of ordinary labor.
Think about that.
Even the servant who received only one talent had been entrusted with something extraordinarily valuable.
He was not given nothing.
He was given a tremendous responsibility.
And this matters because some people have spent years telling themselves they have nothing worth offering.
“I don't have the gift that person has.”
“I don't have the money.”
“I don't have the education.”
“I don't have the platform.”
“I don't know Scripture like other Christians.”
“I can't preach.”
“I can't lead.”
“I can't do anything important for God.”
But notice what Jesus did not say.
He did not say the master expected the servant with one talent to produce the same result as the servant with five.
He did not condemn the servant for receiving less.
The difference in what they received was not the problem.
The problem was what the third servant did with what he had received.
The first servant went and traded with his five talents, gaining five more.
The second did likewise and gained two more.
But the third?
Matthew 25:18 says:
“But he that had received one went and digged in the earth, and hid his lord's money.” (KJV)
Read that again.
He went.
He dug.
He hid.
He was not incapable of taking action.
He took deliberate action to make sure nothing happened with what his master had entrusted to him.
And there is something haunting about that.
Sometimes the energy we spend protecting ourselves from obedience is greater than the energy obedience itself would require.
We spend years constructing explanations.
We rehearse reasons why now is not the right time.
We call fear wisdom.
We call avoidance discernment.
We call spiritual passivity waiting on God.
And sometimes, beneath all those explanations, there is a truth we do not want to confront.
We do not want to risk surrendering control.
Now, Scripture does not teach that every delay is disobedience or that every quiet season is spiritual failure. God often calls His people to wait, rest, heal, and prepare.
But there is a difference between waiting faithfully on the Lord and using the language of faith to excuse a settled refusal to obey Him.
The servant in this parable did not simply need more time.
He had already decided what kind of master he believed he served.
And that decision shaped everything.
When the master returned after a long time, he called his servants to settle accounts.
The first servant came forward with ten talents.
The second came with four.
And both heard the same extraordinary words.
“Well done, thou good and faithful servant.” — Matthew 25:21, 23 (KJV)
Do not miss this.
One servant brought back ten.
Another brought back four.
But the master's praise was the same.
The reward was not based on who possessed the largest amount.
Both were commended for faithfulness.
Both were invited into the joy of their lord.
The kingdom of God does not operate according to the shallow comparisons that dominate our world.
Heaven does not measure faithfulness by follower counts, public applause, bank balances, or how impressive our lives look beside someone else's.
The person quietly caring for an elderly parent in Christ's name may be displaying profound faithfulness.
The believer praying through tears in a hospital room may be honoring God in ways nobody else sees.
The Christian who refuses dishonesty when nobody is watching may be demonstrating obedience that never becomes a public testimony.
The person who faithfully teaches a child the Scriptures may never know how far those seeds will grow.
God sees what the world overlooks.
And faithfulness does not have to be famous to be precious to Him.
But then the third servant stepped forward.
And the atmosphere of the story changed.
He said:

“Lord, I knew thee that thou art an hard man, reaping where thou hast not sown, and gathering where thou hast not strawed: And I was afraid, and went and hid thy talent in the earth: lo, there thou hast that is thine.” — Matthew 25:24–25 (KJV)
There it is.
“I was afraid.”
Three words.
Three words that have imprisoned more lives than many people realize.
I was afraid.
Afraid of failure.
Afraid of criticism.
Afraid of being misunderstood.
Afraid of losing security.
Afraid that obedience might cost something.
Afraid that God might ask for more than I wanted to surrender.
And fear can become especially dangerous when we begin using it to justify disobedience.
But we must be careful here.
Jesus is not condemning every person who experiences fear.
Moses was afraid.
Jeremiah felt inadequate.
The disciples trembled in the storm.
Peter denied Jesus under pressure.
Fear itself does not automatically prove that someone has rejected God.
The issue is what the servant's fear revealed and what he chose to do with it.
He did not bring his fear honestly to the master and seek help.
He used his fear as the defense of a life that had refused its responsibility.
And listen to how he described his master.
“I knew thee that thou art an hard man...”
The Greek phrase includes σκληρὸς ἄνθρωπος (sklēros anthrōpos), meaning a hard or harsh man.
That is the servant's accusation.
It is not necessarily an accurate description of the master, and we should not turn the servant's accusation into a declaration that God is cruel.
In fact, the master's response exposes the inconsistency of the servant's excuse.
If the servant truly believed the master was so demanding, why did he not at least deposit the money with bankers so it could earn interest?
The servant's own reasoning did not justify his behavior.
His words revealed that he had no faithful answer for his inaction.
And this is where the parable becomes more than a story about an ancient household.
Because a distorted view of God can deeply affect how we live before Him.
Some people picture God as perpetually disappointed.
They imagine Him waiting for their next mistake.
They believe that one failure will make Him withdraw His love.
They approach Him like frightened employees trying to avoid punishment rather than repentant sinners learning to trust a gracious Father.
But Jesus Christ reveals the Father's heart.
John 1:14 tells us that the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, full of grace and truth.
Romans 5:8 tells us that God demonstrated His love toward us while we were still sinners.
And 1 John 4:18 teaches that perfect love casts out fear, because fear has to do with punishment.
This does not mean we should abandon reverence for God.
Scripture calls us to fear the Lord in the sense of holy awe, worship, and reverent submission.
But reverence is not the same as believing God is malicious.
And grace is not permission to bury our responsibilities.
The God who welcomes sinners through Jesus Christ is also the holy God who calls His people to follow Him.
Both truths belong together.
Then the master speaks.
And his words are devastating.
“Thou wicked and slothful servant...” — Matthew 25:26 (KJV)
The Greek text uses πονηρὲ δοῦλε καὶ ὀκνηρέ (ponēre doule kai oknēre).
The words identify the servant as wicked and lazy or slothful.
Not merely unsuccessful.
Not simply less productive than the others.
Wicked and slothful.
Why?
Because the issue was never merely the amount of money.
It was his refusal to act faithfully with what belonged to his master.
He had been entrusted with something.
He understood that it belonged to someone else.
He knew his master would return.
And yet he treated the entrusted treasure as something to be hidden away rather than stewarded.
He preserved the possession while neglecting the purpose.
That sentence should make us examine our own hearts.
Because it is possible to preserve the appearance of religion while neglecting the call of discipleship.
You can own a Bible and rarely open it.
You can know the language of Christianity while resisting the Lordship of Christ.
You can defend biblical truth in arguments while refusing to practice mercy.
You can attend church faithfully while refusing to forgive someone.
You can speak passionately about evangelism while remaining indifferent to people who do not know Jesus.
You can be publicly respectable and privately unrepentant.
And none of us should read that as permission to point accusing fingers at someone else.
The first question is not, “Who do I know who needs to hear this?”
The first question is:
“Lord, where have I been hiding from You?”
Perhaps you have been hiding behind a wound.
Someone betrayed you in church.
A leader disappointed you.
A ministry experience left you exhausted.
You trusted someone who used Scripture to manipulate you.
And somewhere along the way, you decided that staying distant was safer than opening your heart again.
If that is your story, your pain deserves to be acknowledged.
Jesus does not ask you to pretend that spiritual abuse was acceptable or that healthy boundaries are sinful.
Faithfulness may include stepping away from harmful environments and seeking healing.
But do not allow the failures of people to convince you that Jesus Himself cannot be trusted.
He is not the one who betrayed you.
He is the Shepherd who laid down His life for His sheep.
Perhaps your hiding looks different.
You know there is a relationship in which you need to seek reconciliation, where it is safe and appropriate.
You know there is a habit you need to bring into the light.
You know there is a sin you keep defending.
You know there is a person you need to stop mistreating.
You know that the faith you profess on Sunday is barely recognizable in your choices throughout the week.
And every time conviction comes, you promise yourself:
“Tomorrow.”
But tomorrow becomes another week.
Another month.
Another year.
And eventually, the grave of buried obedience begins to look like normal life.
That is the tragedy Jesus is exposing.
Not that the servant had only one talent.
But that he buried it.
And before we continue, there is an even deeper truth we cannot afford to miss.
This parable is not teaching that we can earn salvation by producing enough results for God.
If we miss that, we miss the Gospel.
Ephesians 2:8–9 declares that we are saved by grace through faith, not by works, so that no one can boast.
But the very next verse says we are created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared beforehand that we should walk in them.
Grace is the source.
Good works are the fruit.
Faithfulness is not the price we pay to purchase salvation.
It is part of the transformed life that God's saving grace produces.
That distinction matters enormously.
Because a person can hear Matthew 25 and conclude:
“I must do more, achieve more, sacrifice more, and exhaust myself until God finally accepts me.”
That is not the Gospel.
Jesus Christ did not die on the cross so that sinners could spend the rest of their lives trying to earn the forgiveness He freely offers.
He died for sinners who could never save themselves.
He rose again.
And everyone who truly turns to Him in repentance and faith finds mercy that cannot be purchased.
But the same grace that forgives us also begins changing us.
Titus 2:11–12 teaches that the grace of God trains us to renounce ungodliness and live godly lives.
Grace does not leave us comfortably buried in the old life.
Grace calls us out.
And that is why the warning of Matthew 25 is so serious.
The third servant's refusal exposed something deeply wrong in his relationship with the master.
Jesus ends the parable with judgment, not a mild warning about missed opportunities.
The servant is cast into outer darkness.
We should not soften that ending until it loses its meaning.
Within the surrounding teaching about Christ's return, the language is a solemn warning of final exclusion and judgment.
It confronts the danger of merely claiming to belong to the Master without living in faithful response to Him.
But neither should we misuse this passage to terrorize tenderhearted believers who are grieving their failures and sincerely seeking Christ.
The warning is not that one missed opportunity, one season of weakness, or one imperfect act of service automatically proves someone is condemned.
The parable describes a servant whose sustained refusal to act reveals the condition of his heart.
Jesus is calling us to examine whether our profession of faith is real.
And if that examination exposes sin, the answer is not despair.
The answer is repentance.
The answer is Christ.
Because here is the breathtaking difference between the servant's story and the invitation still being offered to you.
You are reading this before your own life has ended.
There is still an opportunity to turn to Jesus.
Still an opportunity to confess what you have hidden.
Still an opportunity to seek forgiveness.
Still an opportunity to obey where you have resisted.
Still an opportunity to stop pretending.
Not because tomorrow is guaranteed.
It is not.
But because today, the Gospel is being proclaimed to you.
And Jesus has not changed.
Remember Peter?
He promised loyalty.
He insisted he would never abandon Jesus.
Then, when pressure came, he denied knowing Him three times.
Imagine the shame.
The sound of the rooster.
The memory of his own words.
The unbearable knowledge that he had failed the One he loved.
If Peter's story ended there, it would be a tragedy.
But after His resurrection, Jesus met Peter again.
In John 21, Jesus questioned Peter about his love and commissioned him to care for His sheep.
Peter's failure was real.
His sin was not excused.
But his failure did not have the final word.
Jesus restored him.
And that restoration did not lead Peter away from responsibility.
It called him into faithful service.
This is the beauty of grace.
Christ does not merely forgive the past.
He transforms the future.
From denial to restoration.
From shame to service.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the sin never happened.
Not by calling darkness light.
Not by telling us that obedience no longer matters.
But by bearing sin at the cross, conquering death through His resurrection, and making sinners new through His saving power.
That is why the Christian life is neither a frantic attempt to earn heaven nor a passive decision to do nothing until Jesus returns.
It is a life of grateful, dependent faithfulness.
We belong to Christ.
What we possess ultimately belongs to Him.
Our time.
Our resources.
Our opportunities.
Our influence.
Our knowledge.
Our relationships.
Our abilities.
Our very lives.
And although the talents in Matthew 25 are monetary amounts, the broader biblical principle of stewardship applies to the many things God entrusts to His people.
First Peter 4:10 teaches believers to use the gifts they have received to serve one another as good stewards of God's varied grace.
So ask yourself something.
What has God entrusted to you?
Maybe you are not called to stand behind a pulpit.
Maybe your assignment is to raise your children in the knowledge of Christ.
Maybe it is to speak honestly about Jesus with a friend who has never understood the Gospel.
Maybe it is to practice integrity in a workplace where dishonesty is normal.
Maybe it is to encourage someone who is slowly losing hope.
Maybe it is to serve faithfully in your local church without anyone knowing your name.
Maybe it is to use your resources generously and wisely.
Maybe it is to repent of a hidden sin before it destroys what you love.
Maybe it is to finally open the Bible that has been sitting beside your bed for months.
You do not need to invent a grand assignment to begin obeying God.
Start with what Scripture has already made clear.
Love God.
Love your neighbor.
Repent of sin.
Trust Jesus.
Speak truth.
Practice mercy.
Pray.
Forgive.
Serve.
Remain faithful.
And do not confuse smallness with insignificance.
The master praised the servant with two talents just as warmly as the servant with five.
That should free someone today.
You do not have to become somebody else to be faithful with what God has entrusted to you.
You do not have to compete with another Christian's calling.
You do not have to become famous.
You do not have to build a platform.
You do not have to prove that you matter by collecting applause.
You are called to follow Jesus.
And the faithfulness that nobody notices is never hidden from God.
Perhaps the most beautiful part of the faithful servants' reward is not the greater responsibility they received.
It is the invitation:
“Enter thou into the joy of thy lord.” — Matthew 25:21 (KJV)
The ultimate treasure is not the talents.
It is the joy of the Master.
The Christian's highest hope is not to stand before Jesus holding a résumé of impressive achievements.
It is to belong to Him.
To see Him.
To dwell with Him.
To rejoice in the One who loved us and gave Himself for us.
And this changes how we think about stewardship.
We do not serve merely because we fear losing everything.
We serve because Christ is worthy of everything.
We do not give because we can buy God's approval.
We give because we have already received grace beyond calculation.
We do not share the Gospel because we are trying to manufacture spiritual trophies.
We share because Jesus Christ is the only Savior, and people need to hear the good news of His death and resurrection.
And perhaps this is where the story needs to become personal.
Because somewhere, right now, someone is holding a phone and reading these words while carrying a quiet conviction they have been avoiding.
They know what they have buried.
Nobody else knows.
Their family does not know.
Their friends do not know.
Their pastor may not know.
But God knows.
And perhaps that person is you.
If it is, you do not need to perform for the people reading the comments.
You do not need to publicly disclose painful details or confess private sins to strangers.
But you can be honest before God.
You can stop defending what He is calling you to surrender.
You can ask Him for mercy.
You can seek help from a trustworthy, mature Christian where needed.
And you can take the next faithful step.
Not ten imaginary steps.
The next real one.
If you are weary but still trusting Christ, you might write:
And if you need prayer, you can simply say:
“Pray for me.”
Not to prove your salvation to anyone.
Not to earn grace through a public response.
But because sometimes a few honest words can open a door for encouragement, prayer, and fellowship.
Pray for them.
Remind them of Scripture.
Help them remember that Christ is sufficient.
That is the kind of community we want Gospel Warrior to cultivate.
Not a crowd that applauds religious performance.
A family of believers who keep pointing one another back to Jesus.
Not because sharing a post makes someone righteous.
Not because a social media algorithm determines spiritual faithfulness.
But because someone among your family, friends, coworkers, or acquaintances may need to hear this message.
Someone may have mistaken fear for wisdom.
Someone may be comparing their one talent with another person's five.
Someone may believe their failure has placed them beyond the reach of grace.
Someone may be outwardly religious while inwardly running from Christ.
You may never know who reads what you share.
But you can prayerfully use the opportunities you have to point others toward the truth.
The goal is not to gather people around a personality.
It is to help people grow in their knowledge of the Savior.
And there is another way you can help this ministry continue.
Gospel Warrior exists to proclaim Jesus Christ, teach the Scriptures, encourage struggling believers, and make discipleship resources more accessible.
We want these resources to reach more people.
The exhausted parent searching for biblical encouragement after everyone else has gone to sleep.
The young believer trying to understand Scripture.
The person recovering from a painful season who needs to rediscover the hope of the Gospel.
The Christian who wants to move beyond occasional inspiration and develop a deeper, more disciplined walk with Jesus.
And the seeker who has questions about who Christ really is.
Creating, maintaining, and expanding a ministry like this requires time, labor, resources, and the generous support of people who believe the work is worthwhile.
It is not a requirement for salvation.
It does not purchase forgiveness, spiritual status, or special favor with Christ.
And it should never replace the biblical responsibilities you already have toward your family, your local church, or those in genuine need.
Scripture teaches that supporting faithful Gospel ministry is good and appropriate.
Galatians 6:6 speaks about sharing good things with those who teach the Word.
Philippians 4:15–18 describes the Philippian believers' financial partnership with Paul in the work of the Gospel.
And 2 Corinthians 9:7 reminds us that giving should not be reluctant or under compulsion, because God loves a cheerful giver.
This is the spirit in which we ask.
Not pressure.
Not guilt.
Not a promise that giving money will guarantee material prosperity.
A willing partnership in the work of making biblical teaching and discipleship resources available to more people.
What matters is that your giving is sincere, responsible, and directed toward the glory of God.
These products are not the heart of the ministry.
Jesus is.
You are welcome to keep reading, learning, praying, and growing with us.
The Gospel is not for sale.
And the Word of God must never be treated as a product that only paying supporters deserve to hear.
But Christ alone saves the soul.
That is the distinction we will never compromise.
Now, return with me one last time to that servant standing before his master.
Imagine the soil beneath his fingernails.
Imagine the place where he dug.
Imagine the moment he decided that hiding the treasure was safer than faithfully using it.
Imagine the years passing while the money remained buried.
Then imagine the day the master returned.
Suddenly, the hiding place could not protect him.
The explanation could not justify him.
And the money he had preserved could not make up for the faithfulness he had refused.
That is the unsettling truth of Matthew 25.
The servant's tragedy was not that he had too little. It was that he refused to be faithful with what he had.
But please do not leave this story looking only at the servant.
Look to the greater Master.
Look to Jesus Christ.
The One who told this parable would soon go to the cross.
The sinless Son of God would be rejected, mocked, scourged, and crucified.
He would bear the judgment that sinners deserve.
And on the third day, He would rise from the grave.
The empty tomb declares that death does not have the final word over those who belong to Him.
That is where Christian hope begins.
Not in our productivity.
Not in our religious reputation.
Not in the amount of money we give.
Not even in the strength of our own promises.
Our hope rests in the crucified and risen Savior.
And because He lives, repentance is not the end of your story.
It can be the beginning of a transformed life.
You may have wasted years.
You may have hidden behind excuses.
You may have neglected opportunities.
You may have made decisions you deeply regret.
You may be carrying the painful consequences of disobedience.
But if you are hearing His call today, do not respond by trying to bargain with God.
Come to Christ.
Confess your sin.
Trust His finished work.
Ask Him to change your heart.
Then walk in the obedience that flows from faith.
And remember that God is not asking you to produce another person's harvest.
He calls you to be faithful with what He has entrusted to you.
Perhaps that means beginning again with a trembling prayer.
Perhaps it means telling the truth.
Perhaps it means returning to Scripture.
Perhaps it means serving someone quietly.
Perhaps it means turning away from a cherished sin.
Perhaps it means finally saying:
“Lord, I have been afraid. But I do not want fear to rule my life anymore. Teach me to trust You.”
You do not have to make that prayer sound impressive.
God is not impressed by polished words that conceal an unwilling heart.
Come honestly.
Come humbly.
Come through Jesus Christ.
And if this article has reached something deep within you, I would love to hear what part of Matthew 25 challenged you most.
Was it the servant's fear?
The way he viewed his master?
The fact that both faithful servants received the same praise?
Or the realization that the greatest danger may not always be losing what we have, but refusing to steward it faithfully?
Not to shame them.
To invite them to the same grace that you need.
Because every one of us stands in need of Jesus.
The most important question is not whether we can impress the Master with a great performance.
It is whether we truly belong to Him, trust His grace, and respond to His call with living faith.
One day, the waiting will end.
One day, the Master will return.
And the things we treated as permanent will be revealed as temporary.
May we be found trusting Christ.
May our faith be genuine.
May our lives bear the fruit of His grace.
And may our greatest joy be hearing the welcome of the Lord who redeemed us.
Do not spend your life guarding the grave of what God entrusted to you, when Christ is calling you to walk in the light.
